newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais investment certificates soar.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais investment certificates soar.

text.p: Investors piled into Credit Lyonnais on Friday, pushing its investment certificates up nearly 10 percent after soon-to-be privatised Thomson-CSF said it would get more than two billion francs ($360 million) for its stake in the struggling French state-controlled bank.
Thomson-CSF, the defence electronics arm of electronics giant Thomson SA, announced the state would pay it 2.34 billion francs for its roughly 18 percent stake in the bank.
The investment certificates in Credit Lyonnais soared on market speculation that minority shareholders might seek to be bought out at the same level when the government privatises the bank.
The certificates, which make up 21 percent of the bank's capital but carry no voting rights, finished up 16.90 francs at 186.60 francs.

The price for Thomson-CSF's stake in Credit Lyonnais was based on the bank's December 1995 share price of 306.70 francs. That translated into a value for the bank's investment certificates of 274 francs.
The price was set following an evaluation by investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Thomson-CSF said.

The bank's investment certificates, floated in 1986 at just under 700 francs, have been in a downward spiral since a reckless expansion spree in the late 1980s and early 1990s resulted in massive losses.
But of late they have been rising on hopes sparked by the centre-right government's plans to privatise the bank but analysts regard the certificates as a speculative play.
The government has said it plans to sell the bank as soon as possible but the bank has said it believes such a move is unlikely before next year.
Thomson-CSF made the statement after a spate of newspaper articles speculating about the sale price for its stake in the bank.
Last month, the European Commission announced it would open a formal probe into the repurchase by the French state of Thomson-CSF's stake in the bank.

Commission officials said in December the Commission would have to assess whether the acquisition of Thomson's stake by the state was being made above the market price which could amount to a disguised state subsidy.
But Thomson-CSF said, "The payment of this amount of 2.34 million francs...will be carried out in concert between the French authorities and the European Commission."

The government is expected to announce its decision on the sale of its stake in Thomson-CSF before the end of February after being forced to suspect a previous privatisation attempt late last year. ($1=5.572 French Franc)
